item.title: 'Dancing' two-dimensional patterns in nematics above the flexoelectric instability threshold
item.description: arXiv:2610.31849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Various types of electrohydrodynamic instabilities in liquid crystals (LCs) are a recurring theme in LC research. The nonlinear stage of the flexoelectric instability in nematics remains the least studied aspect of this phenomenon. This work highlights a key advancement in nonlinear physics, providing a compelling example of nonlinear dynamical system behavior. By solving the system of nonlinear equations for a nematic in an alternating external field, we derive from first principles the unique "dancing" behavior of truly two-dimensional patterns above the flexoelectric instability threshold. Our analysis is restricted to liquid crystals with negative dielectric permittivity and electrical conductivity anisotropies. The resulting solution represents a stable limit cycle near above the Hopf bifurcation, valid within the parameters range where the solutions characteristic exponent is complex. The generalized two-dimensional Ginzburg-Landau-like phenomenological theory of the phenomenon is developed.
item.dc:creator: E. S. Pikina

item.title: Spatiotemporally-resolved differential dynamic microscopy reveals strain-induced deformations in heterogeneous soft materials
item.description: arXiv:2610.32005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding the microscopic behavior of materials in response to mechanical perturbations is a central challenge in soft matter, yet existing methods, which typically rely on microscopy-based imaging, often struggle with spatial heterogeneity and low signal-to-noise that are characteristic of many soft and biological materials. Additionally, many existing rheo-optical methods focus on the response to macro-scale forces rather than localized perturbations despite the importance of local stresses in biological and industrial applications of soft materials. Here, we present STroboscopically Averaged, time-Resolved Differential Dynamic Microscopy (starDDM) to investigate a sample's deformation across time and distance due to a cyclically applied local force. As proof-of-principle, we use this model-independent and tracer-free approach to map the motions of active cytoskeleton composites imposed by the movement of an optically trapped probe particle embedded within the complex network. We reveal how motor-driven restructuring and varying strain rates tune the magnitude and propagation of the response, which we further show decays with distance from the perturbation. This analytical platform fills a critical gap in micro-rheology, offering a versatile tool for probing the non-equilibrium dynamics of soft materials ranging from biopolymer networks to 3D-printed materials and soft robotics.
item.dc:creator: Aysan Razzaghi, Mehrzad Sasanpour, Jasmine Ren, Caidric Gupit, Matthew E. Helgeson, Megan T. Valentine, Rae M. Robertson-Anderson, Ryan McGorty

item.title: Machine Learning Accelerated Simulation of Charge Regulation Effects
item.description: arXiv:2610.32713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many solvated materials, from nanoparticles to polyelectrolytes, acquire charge through the dissociation or association of surface groups, a phenomenon known as charge regulation (CR). Recent methods use hybrid charge regulation Monte Carlo (CR-MC)/molecular dynamics (MD) to evolve the system while dynamically adjusting charges on the surface groups. However, this approach is computationally expensive, as Monte Carlo sampling can be as costly as the accompanying MD. In this work, we introduce charge regulation machine learning (CR-ML), a graph attention network that predicts the ionization probability of every surface site from the instantaneous configuration, the dissociation constant of surface groups, and the solution conditions. We show that CR-ML reproduces the equilibrium conformations and degree of ionization obtained with CR-MC for a hydrophobic polyanion. We further test CR-ML on the more complex system of two nanoparticles mediated by a polyelectrolyte, where it accurately predicts the charge asymmetry that develops between the two particles. Across these systems, CR-ML updates charges an order of magnitude faster than CR-MC while accurately reproducing its equilibrium properties. This framework opens a path toward large-scale simulations of charge-regulating materials for understanding and designing their responsive behavior.
item.dc:creator: Vijay Yadav, Sunita Kumari, Prabhat K. Jaiswal

item.title: Field Directed Assembly of Anisotropic Composite Pacman Colloids into Reconfigurable Architectures
item.description: arXiv:2610.32872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the field-directed assembly of patchy colloidal particles composed of magnetic hematite cubes encapsulated in TPM shells. These Pacman-like particles exhibit specific interactions via their magnetic patch, enabling tunable structures under external fields. A magnetic field drives patch-to-patch interactions, while an AC electric field induces stacking and spreading. By using this multi-field combination and by varying field parameters, such as frequency and amplitude, we achieve programmable transitions between distinct assembly modes. Our work offers a versatile platform for designing reconfigurable colloidal architectures with potential applications in micro-robotics and smart materials.
item.dc:creator: Indira Barros, Isha Songara, Indrani Chakraborty

item.title: Time-temperature superposition from multi-temperature chirp rheometry of thermorheologically simple materials via physics-informed Gaussian processes
item.description: arXiv:2610.32895v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inferring constitutive laws from transient response data is a central inverse problem in soft condensed-matter physics, particularly when the relevant relaxation spectrum extends beyond the time window of a single experiment. Time-temperature superposition (TTS) constrains this problem for thermorheologically simple materials in the linear viscoelastic regime by allowing temperature to rescale the characteristic relaxation time without changing the underlying shape of the relaxation spectrum. We incorporate this constraint into a physics-informed machine-learning framework for time-resolved mechanical spectroscopy via chirp rheometry. We encode compact fractional viscoelastic models as causal convolutional features derived from the Boltzmann superposition principle, and we jointly fit multi-temperature chirp records using sparse variational Gaussian process regression. The model infers horizontal shift factors, constitutive parameters, and an observational-noise scale directly from time-domain stress-strain signals measured in the linear viscoelastic regime, without first extracting frequency-domain spectra or manually shifting separate curves. For synthetic Fractional Maxwell data, the method recovers the generating constitutive law from a prescribed model library and latent shifts over stress-noise levels from 3% to 25%. Applied to a DGEBA-IPDA epoxy dataset spanning the glass-transition regime, the pooled likelihood distinguishes competing fractional rheology models using the Bayesian information criterion. These results recast TTS master-curve construction as probabilistic inference over latent time rescaling and linear viscoelasticity, while also identifying limitations, such as homoscedastic noise and weakly informative spectral regimes.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Y. Miranda-Valdez, Kourosh Mobredi, Juha Koivisto, Mikko J. Alava

item.title: Folding of Free Polymers Under Confinement by Responsive Hydrogels
item.description: arXiv:2610.32912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Controlling the folding of biopolymers in crowded and confined environments, such as the interior of biological cells, remains a significant challenge. Macromolecular crowding and spatial confinement can strongly influence transition pathways between folded and unfolded states of proteins. Such environments can be mimicked in experiments by confining polymers within soft, tunable media, such as hydrogels -- cross-linked polymer networks that swell by absorbing solvent and exhibit stimulus-dependent responsiveness. Here, we develop a self-consistent mean-field theory for the equilibrium swelling and internal composition of a hydrogel immersed in a solution of free polymer coils. The theory extends the Flory-Rehner framework by incorporating free polymer coils, modeled as fluctuating ellipsoids, whose sizes and shapes are characterized by the eigenvalues of the gyration tensor. Confinement of the coils within gel pores is characterized by an effective free-volume fraction, parametrized from numerical calculations for self-avoiding-walk chains between hard walls. Coupled chemical potential equilibrium conditions are solved numerically over ranges of coil molecular weight and free polymer concentration. We find that free polymers drive a non-monotonic swelling response of hydrogels, with osmotic swelling at low concentrations followed by deswelling at higher concentrations, in qualitative agreement with experiment. We further demonstrate that confinement within gel pores reduces the radius of gyration and asphericity of embedded polymer coils, driving them toward compact, globular conformations analogous to folded protein states. These results establish a theoretical foundation for using responsive hydrogels as tunable, artificial chaperone-like systems capable of inducing and controlling biopolymer folding.
item.dc:creator: Mahesh Aryal, Alan R. Denton

item.title: CBTV: Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry for Dense Granular Flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.31883v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conventional particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) has been the standard diagnostic tool for studying fluid and granular flows. However, in dense granular systems, the average distance moved by particles between frames can approach or exceed inter-particle spacing, demanding ultra-high frame rates. Furthermore, neighbouring particles may move together, and common velocity-based prediction fails after energetic collisions. Existing methods struggle to track granular particles without losing identities or swapping. We present Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry (CBTV), a training-free multi-pass method leveraging multicoloured particles to achieve enhanced tracking. CBTV first matches constellations of neighbouring coloured particles as single units, guided by a cross-correlation motion prior, and only then assigns the remaining particles individually. We compare it with 12 baseline tracker configurations, from classical linkers to graph-neural-network and transformer models, on 59 cases from 15 simulated discrete-element granular flows with exact ground truth (0.006-9 diameters/frame). CBTV matches or exceeds every tracker tested on an impulsive collision at every displacement. Its advantage lies in dense flows in which particles move between about half and twice their spacing per frame, where links between frames are ambiguous. On agitated shear flow, a colour relaxation tracker, which also uses neighbour context, matches or narrowly exceeds CBTV. Where links are unambiguous, CBTV is close to the best tracker, and beyond about two to three particle diameters per frame, the range of its motion prior, trackers that compensate for bulk motion are more accurate. For experimentalists, dense granular flows of coloured particles can be tracked at displacements per frame where trackers without neighbour context lose identities, easing the demand for ultra-high frame rates without training data.
item.dc:creator: Kaveeshan Thurairajah, Zhao Pan

item.title: Sub-monolayer tracking of molecular states at buried interfaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.31924v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Phenomena responsible for emerging technologies originate from novel molecular states at buried interfaces. Yet quantitatively resolving these features is out of reach in most cases. Resonant scattering has demonstrated sensitivity to these local states but is limited due to a lack of accurate interpretive models. We leverage a machine learning (ML)-optimized optical model to analyze polarized resonant soft X-ray scattering (RSoXS) from molecular thin films. This new analysis establishes the direct and quantitative interpretation of molecular orientation, chemical identity and packing states as a function of depth with sub-monolayer resolution - reaching beyond the diffraction limit via locking energy and polarization through the optical model. From our analysis, we discover a gradient evolution of molecular orientation and packing emerging from the interface, indicative of competing surface versus bulk growth dynamics and contradicting hypotheses of substrate patterning. This nondestructive insight into buried interfacial formation and final state opens possibilities in controlling interfacial states and phenomena in next-generation technologies.
item.dc:creator: Harlan Heilman, Em Biegler, Sushil Adhikari, Victor Murcia, Tanner Melody, Fred Woodall, Lars Thomsen, Obaid Alqahtani, Brian A. Collins

item.title: Boundary shape controls the stress distribution in two-component elastic materials
item.description: arXiv:2610.32072v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate how the shape and arrangement of high-stiffness regions govern stress redistribution in two-component triangular elastic spring networks subjected to spatially correlated and uncorrelated random prestress. We compare boundary roughness, partitioning into disconnected regions, and graded transitions between regions of different stiffness. Our simulations identify interface bonds as channels for energy transfer: increasing their number provides additional transfer paths and reduces stress concentration in mechanically rigid regimes, while offering little benefit in compliant subnetworks. This is analogous to defects in naturally occurring crystal structures, where the defects themselves isolate stress. At a fixed fraction of high-stiffness material, partitioning reduces stress concentration for both correlated and uncorrelated prestress. The benefit diminishes with further subdivision as the number of interface bonds becomes comparable to the number of interior nodes. Stress reduction, however, depends on the spatial correlations of the imposed prestress: random prestress generally yields a stronger effect, though the difference diminishes in some regimes. Graded interfaces further reduce peak stress by distributing the stiffness transition over a broader region. Together, these results suggest design strategies based on increasing interface area, matching subdivision scale to prestress correlations, and grading stiffness transitions. This minimal framework identifies how internal structure controls energy transfer and stress redistribution, suggesting design principles for mechanical robustness under both internal and external loading.
item.dc:creator: Kyungeun Kim, Adam Clare, Miranda Holmes-Cerfon

item.title: Multi-scale patterns arising from competing chemotactic interactions
item.description: arXiv:2610.32591v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Classical chemotaxis models consider the directed motion of cells in response to a chemical gradient. Recent experiments suggest that biological microswimmers such as bacteria can perform chemotaxis toward multiple chemicals, which dynamically evolve depending on the distribution of the microswimmers. In this Letter, we consider a mass-conserving chemotaxis model in which pattern formation is driven by two competing chemicals, autoinducers and nutrients, where the former acts as an activator and the latter as an inhibitor for coarsening. We show that this can give rise to diverse patterns including long wavelength uninterrupted coarsening, Turing-like arrested coarsening, traveling waves as well as a novel class of mixed multi-scale oscillatory coarsening patterns, where a dense aggregate coexist with a dynamically spreading part of the population. We analytically derive the conditions for the onset of such patterns and discuss their physical implications, which significantly broadens our understanding of signaling active matter and pattern formation in general.
item.dc:creator: Agniva Datta, Robert Gro{\ss}mann, Carsten Beta

item.title: Ginzburg-Landau Theory with Elastic Incompatibility Describes the Liquid-G-phase-Crystal State Diagram
item.description: arXiv:2610.32791v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We derive a mechanically consistent Ginzburg-Landau theory for the metastable heterogeneous G state reported in deeply undercooled metallic liquids. The central result is that type-II-like mixed-state physics can emerge structurally with the random internal stress field playing the role of the magnetic field. Frozen eigenstrain due to elastic incompatibility between ordered cores and the amorphous matrix generates incompatible stress, while the non-affine internal strain in the liquid-like matrix in between the ordered cores relaxes that stress over a finite screening length $\lambda_\sigma$ (analogous to the London length in the superconducting problem). Structural order heals over a distinct mechanically-dressed length $\xi_G$; their ratio $\kappa_G=\lambda_\sigma/\xi_G$ provides the structural counterpart of the Ginzburg-Landau parameter. Because the matrix is transiently rigid yet locally relaxational only over an intermediate time window, the same mechanism selects crystal for slow protocols, a heterogeneous G state at intermediate rates, and a homogeneous L-like glass under rapid arrest. Residual incompatibility frustrates coarsening, allowing finite ordered cores and screened, orientation-dependent core interactions. The resulting texture is an inverted Abrikosov analogue: structural order resides in the cores, whereas incompatible-stress screening is carried by the surrounding disordered matrix. The theory yields direct simulation and experimental tests through stress-decay, structural-healing, non-affine-susceptibility, and kinetic measurements.
item.dc:creator: Alessio Zaccone, Konrad Samwer

item.title: Ideal interaction dynamics of defects and background fields in condensed matter
item.description: arXiv:2610.32973v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While defect dynamics in condensed matter systems is widely studied and several methods are available to track the defect position over time, the formulation of dynamical models for the coupled evolution of both defect and background field quantities seems to be more challenging. Yet, the overall behavior of a system containing moving defects is strongly influenced by this defect-field interaction. Here, we propose a modeling framework for the conservative coupled evolution of the defect density and the background fields upon focusing on two relevant cases of study: the Gross-Pitaevskii theory of quantum fluids and the Ericksen-Leslie model of nematic liquid crystals. To achieve the coupled evolution, we combine the Euler-Poincar\'e variational setting of continuum dynamics with the gauge theory of topological defects. While the latter allows us to overcome certain ambiguities in definition of the defect density, the Euler-Poincar\'e method provides a unified modeling approach in the absence of defect reconnection.
item.dc:creator: Fran\c{c}ois Gay-Balmaz, Tudor S. Ratiu, Cesare Tronci

item.title: Flexoelectricity-driven softening of bend elasticity leads to spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking in a polar fluid
item.description: arXiv:2602.15687v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The origin of the recently observed spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking in polar fluids composed of achiral molecules is an unsolved problem, raising fundamental questions about how heliconical structures emerge in such systems. Here, we investigate the pretransitional fluctuations leading to the formation of the spontaneously chiral twist-bend ferroelectric nematic phase using dielectric spectroscopy, light scattering, and small-angle X-ray scattering. We observe simultaneous softening of the bend elastic constant and the emergence of a collective dielectric mode on approaching the transition. By developing a theoretical model, we show that these phenomena are signatures of a flexoelectricity-driven transition arising from the coupling between electric polarization and bend deformation.
item.dc:creator: Aitor Erkoreka, Josu Martinez-Perdiguero, Luka Cmok, Ema Han\v{z}el, Jordan Hobbs, Calum J. Gibb, Richard J. Mandle, Nerea Sebasti\'an, Alenka Mertelj

item.title: Dissipation and microstructure in sheared active suspensions of squirmers
item.description: arXiv:2603.00392v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the energy expenditure and structural correlations in semi-dilute to concentrated suspensions of squirmers using active fast Stokesian dynamics simulations. Specifically, we simulate apolar active suspensions of squirmers, or 'shakers,' and show that shear enhances the total dissipation but reduces the relative viscosity for both puller- and pusher-type shakers. At low shear rates where activity dominates, hydrodynamic interactions increase the active dissipation, more so for pullers at higher volume fractions, whereas pushers exhibit a higher viscosity, in contrast to bacterial suspensions displaying a 'superfluid' transition. At high shear rates where shear dominates, pullers and pushers behave effectively as passive spheres, generating negative normal stress differences due to shear-induced collision. Remarkably, the rate-dependent rheological responses are accompanied by unusual microstructural signatures of an enhanced nematic order and anisotropic pair correlation, both of which contribute to a higher viscosity under shear. Further simulations of self-propelled, neutral squirmers exhibit similar but weaker shear-thinning, highlighting the importance of activity over motility, underpinned by hydrodynamic interactions. Overall, our results elucidate the interplay of internal activity and external flow on the dissipation and microstructure in sheared active suspensions of squirmers.
item.dc:creator: Zhouyang Ge, Gwynn J. Elfring

item.title: Analyzing the Gelation Transition through Fractional Viscoelasticity and the Mittag-Leffler-Prabhakar Function
item.description: arXiv:2606.26656v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The gelation transition, a process that transforms a flowable liquid into an elastic solid, occurs in a variety of systems, ranging from colloidal to polymeric. During the gelation transition, a system passes through a critical gel state characterized by scale-free power-law viscoelasticity. Interestingly, the fractional calculus provides a natural mathematical language for such power-law viscoelasticity. In this work, we develop physically constrained fractional viscoelastic models, as well as those based on the three-parameter Mittag-Leffler-Prabhakar function, for both the pre-gel and post-gel regimes, ensuring consistency with the conventional scaling relations in each regime. While the fractional pre-gel model is observed to be valid only for a restricted subset of parameter values, the Prabhakar function-based model for the relaxation modulus, which translates into a Havriliak-Negami function-based complex modulus, rigorously removes this limitation. We enforce continuity of the dynamic moduli and their derivatives across the critical gel point, which universally imposes a symmetry in the relaxation dynamics on either side of the critical gel state. Such enforcement further validates the hyperscaling relation connecting the critical exponents, making it a theoretical necessity rather than an empirical coincidence. We validate the proposed models against time- and frequency-domain experimental data. A model-agnostic, frequency-independent rheological fingerprint of the critical gel state, uniquely determined by two critical exponents, is also identified.
item.dc:creator: Yogesh M Joshi

item.title: A neural density functional for polymer electrolytes with exact structure and transferable Coulomb coupling
item.description: arXiv:2610.12132v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ion correlations set the structure of polymer electrolytes and depend on the host permittivity, which is low and varies between polymers. A functional that carries these correlations from molecular simulations to larger inhomogeneous systems must transfer across domain sizes, geometries and coupling strengths. We introduce a neural density functional for the ions of a salt-doped polymer melt with built-in integrability, continuous spatial symmetry, the Noether identities, perfect screening in stable bulk states, and parameters that refer to no grid or box. The permittivity enters only through the Bjerrum length, an explicit argument constrained by an exact relation: the free-energy derivative with respect to the Bjerrum length is the Coulomb correlation energy. Trained by force matching on planar profiles at five Bjerrum lengths spanning 8-30 monomer diameters, the functional predicts, without retraining, density profiles in fourfold longer boxes and under two-dimensional fields, bulk structure factors and the long-wavelength number response, also at a concentration and a permittivity left out of training. It reproduces this energy identity on Coulomb energies that never enter the training. Its nonlinear density dependence captures correlations that a quadratic pair closure misses: the number response grows several-fold with concentration, and at low concentration the coupling lowers it through ion association, below the ideal value at the strongest coupling, while the host sets it in the concentrated melt. At fixed coupling, it is more accurate than three neural architectures and loses little accuracy with a quarter of the training data.
item.dc:creator: Liyao Lyu

item.title: Solubility of poorly soluble species in bulk and nanopores from grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.16599v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Poorly soluble species can have mean populations below one in small systems such as nanopores. In this regime, the grand-potential minimum, which identifies the most probable particle number, differs from the ensemble-averaged solute loading. We use grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling (GCWLS) to calculate the density of states $\Omega(N_\mathrm{A}, N_\mathrm{B})$ for a binary Lennard-Jones mixture of solute B in solvent A, both in bulk and in slit pores. One set of GCWLS simulations gives ensemble averages over a range of chemical potentials, whereas conventional grand-canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulation requires a separate simulation at each state point. Independent GCMC simulations confirm the GCWLS ensemble averages. The solvent number distribution is nearly Gaussian, whereas the dilute solute distribution is skewed and Poisson-like. The most probable solute number therefore lies below the ensemble-averaged loading $\langle N_\mathrm{B}\rangle$ and is zero whenever $\langle N_\mathrm{B}\rangle<1$. Reading the solute loading from the grand-potential minimum underestimates it and can falsely indicate that no solute is present. Defining the oversolubility as $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}=x_\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{conf}}/x_\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{bulk}}$, where $x_\mathrm{B}$ is the solute mole fraction, we find $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}\approx12$ in a pore of 3.5 particle diameters width when both wall interactions are repulsive. Adding wall-solute attraction moderately raises it to $\approx13$, whereas wall-solvent attraction lowers it to $\approx3.4$. This comparison shows that the wall-solvent interaction controls most of the enhancement. As the pore widens, $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}$ decreases toward unity. In bulk and in nanopores alike, the solubility of poorly soluble species should be obtained from ensemble averages rather than from grand-potential minima.
item.dc:creator: Russell Kajouri, Adyant Agrawal, Philipp St\"ark, Alexander Schlaich, Christian Holm

item.title: Soft elasticity of soft shells
item.description: arXiv:2610.27263v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Soft modes of a shell are one-parameter families of non-trivial deformations that preserve the elastic energy. We identify all soft modes of the soft shells described by the variational theory of put forward by Sonnet and Virga (2025). They are seen to be strictly connected with the Bonnet families, a special class of solutions to the problem posited by Bonnet, who asked whether there exist non-trivial isometries that preserve the mean curvature. Differential geometry deems as equivalent all surfaces in one and the same Bonnet family, but continuum mechanics is interested more specifically in soft deformation modes and the shapes they traverse, as they may describe ways to ignite fluctuations of soft shells that ideally require no energy to be activated. We give a general criterion for the existence of soft modes and a method to construct them based on a cascade of path integrations. We apply both criterion and method to some exemplary cases.
item.dc:creator: Andre M. Sonnet, Epifanio G. Virga

item.title: Cell size heterogeneity controls crystallization of the developing fruit fly wing
item.description: arXiv:2505.05437v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A fundamental question in biology is to understand how patterns and shapes emerge from the collective interplay of large numbers of cells. Cells forming two-dimensional epithelial tissues behave as active materials that undergo remodeling and spontaneous shape changes. Focusing on the fly wing as a model system, we find that the cellular packing in the wing epithelium transitions from a disordered packing to an ordered, crystalline packing. While previous studies propose a role of tissue shear flow in establishing the ordered cell packing in the fly wing, we reveal a role of cell size heterogeneity. Indeed, we find that even if tissue shear have been inhibited, cell packings in the fruit fly wing epithelium transition from disordered to an ordered packing. We propose that the transition is controlled by the cell size heterogeneity, which is quantified by the cell size polydispersity. To explore the role of cell size polydispersity in controlling cellular packings, we implement polydispersity in a vertex model of epithelial tissues. Through numerical simulations of this model, we show that there is a critical value of cell size polydispersity above which cellular packings are disordered and below which they form a crystalline packing. By analyzing experimental data, we find that cell size polydispersity decreases during fly wing development. The observed dynamics of tissue crystallisation is consistent with the slow ordering kinetics we observe in the vertex model. Therefore, although tissue shear does not control the transition, it significantly enhances the rate of tissue-scale ordering by facilitating alignment of locally ordered crystallites. Our results identify cell size heterogeneity as a control parameter, in both the vertex model and the fruit fly wing epithelium, controlling the transition between ordered and disordered cellular packings.
item.dc:creator: Kartik Chhajed, Franz S. Gruber, Rapha\"el Etournay, Natalie A. Dye, Frank J\"ulicher, Marko Popovi\'c

item.title: Thermoelastic wave-based logic for mechanically cognitive materials
item.description: arXiv:2511.00647v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent advances in metamaterials and fabrication techniques have revived interest in mechanical computing. Contrary to techniques relying on static deformations of buckling beams or origami-based lattices, the integration of wave scattering and mechanical memory presents a promising path toward efficient, low-latency elastoacoustic computing. This work introduces a novel class of multifunctional mechanical computing circuits that leverage the rich dynamics of phononic and locally resonant materials. These circuits incorporate memory-integrated components, realized here via metamaterial cells infused with shape memory alloys which recall stored elastic profiles and trigger specific actions upon thermal activation. A critical advantage of this realization is its synergistic interaction with incident vibroacoustic loads and the inherited high speed of waves, as opposed to recent adaptations of mechanically intelligent systems that employ innately slower mechanisms such as elastomeric shape changes and snap-through bistabilities. Through a proof-of-concept physical implementation, the efficacy and reconfigurability of the wave-based gates are demonstrated via output probes and measured wavefields. Furthermore, the modular design of the fundamental gates can be used as building blocks to construct complex combinational logic circuits, paving the way for sequential logic in wave-based analog computing systems.
item.dc:creator: Ethan Fort, Mohamed Mousa, Mostafa Nouh

item.title: Uniaxial poroelastic tendon model with crimped fibre recruitment reveals hysteresis
item.description: arXiv:2606.24393v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Fibre recruitment plays an important role in tendon. Due to their large water content, a popular modelling approach for tendons is poroelasticity. Within this framework some tendon studies have included fibres, though none have included crimped fibre recruitment. We present a one dimensional poroelastic model in which the solid skeleton is composed of a soft neo-Hookean background matrix and crimped fibrils which do not bear load (FIB model). As the tissue is stretched, fibrils are straightened and contribute to load bearing. The fibre-reinforced tissue is compared to a tissue with a purely neo-Hookean (NH) skeleton in response to a uniaxial constant applied load (loading) and release of the load (unloading). The system dynamics are governed by a diffusion equation where the diffusion coefficient depends on stiffness. Within tendon parameter ranges, the FIB model is softer than the NH model, and so approaches steady state more slowly during loading. The presence of stiff, crimped fibrils increases bulk extension without excessively straining the fibrils, providing a natural protection mechanism for the tendon's structural components to load, in agreement with experiments. During unloading, the FIB model is much slower to relax as the tissue softens due to fibril re-crimping. This asymmetry in loading and unloading manifests as a hysteresis loop in the stress-strain curve averaged over the tendon. The hysteresis is reduced with increasing applied load. To the authors' knowledge, the finding of hysteresis within this framework is novel. The inclusion of fibrils allows for clearer biological interpretation and potential comparison to data. While the stress law employed in this study is bespoke for the application at hand by accounting for crimp and fibril recruitment, other fibril constitutive laws can readily be considered and incorporated into this framework.
item.dc:creator: Zoe C. Godard, Sarah L. Waters, Derek E. Moulton

item.title: How do incorrect ligands help detect a correct ligand?
item.description: arXiv:2609.25708v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Intrigued by the response of T cell receptors to the presence of a few agonist ligands, we propose a minimal model that can achieve similar performance. The model consists of a small cluster of immobile receptors that bind reversibly to two types (correct/incorrect) of ligands in the environment, with slightly weaker binding strength for the incorrect one. It features binding-state coupling between nearest-neighbor receptors, and receptors in the bound/free states are activated/deactivated by specific enzymes, with rates that allow kinetic proofreading. It is found that, for a range of binding-state coupling strength, incorrect ligands alone cannot activate the receptors, but the binding of merely one correct ligand to a receptor is sufficient to promote the activation of other receptors via induced binding to incorrect ligands. Both response time and signal amplification increase as the receptor binding-state coupling strength increases until it reaches an optimal range to achieve the most rapid and sensitive response. These results suggest a possible mechanism for a speedy and specific response of receptors to very few correct ligands in biological and artificial systems at the subcellular scale.
item.dc:creator: Yan-Ru Chen, Kwan-tai Leung, Hsuan-Yi Chen
